stage-split: The DiT takes 86 to 98 percent of every edit request. Percent of each request's total time, official pipeline, bf16, batch 1. Total seconds at right. One NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (95 GiB), PyTorch 2.14.1, CUDA 13.0. Warm p50 of 5 Turbo and 3 base requests. The unfilled end of each bar is other overhead, under 3 %. VAE encode and decode are summed.
request-latency: Turbo is 4.0 to 4.1 x faster than base, end to end. Seconds per edit request, warm p50, official pipeline, batch 1. At 2048 an edit costs 6.4 to 6.6 times its 1024 time. Each request includes the VAE encode of the input image. One RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, bf16.
prefix-cache: After the first step, the prefix cache halves each DiT step: 523 ms to 259 ms. DiT milliseconds per denoising step, edit at 1024, Turbo (8 steps), official pipeline. Step 1 computes the prefix either way. Steps 2 to 8 are averaged. Whole request: 2.72 s with the cache, 4.57 s without.
utilisation: DiT steps in an edit run at 65 to 71 percent of the card's measured matmul speed. Achieved TFLOP/s per denoising step after the first, official pipeline, bf16. Against the model-shaped matmul (378.5 TFLOP/s) the same steps reach 73 to 80 percent. One RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
peak-memory: The lean port needs 5.4 to 21.4 GiB less at peak. Peak GPU memory in GiB during one Turbo (8 steps) edit, batch 1, text encoder loaded. Dotted line: resident weights, 30.2 GiB. Dashed: the 32 GB RTX 5090, plotted as 32 GiB, and this card at 95.0 GiB. With the text encoder on the card the lowest lean-port peak, 33.5 GiB, still misses 32 GB.
op-groups: Matmul is 55 percent of op time; elementwise, casts and copies cost 1.3 times attention. Milliseconds of GPU time in one Turbo edit request at 1024, by operation group. Turbo, official pipeline, one profiled request (torch profiler, top 30 ops). Shares are of the four groups' 2578 ms sum.
span-split: Attention grows from 19 to 44 percent of an edit's GPU time at 2048. Percent of GPU kernel time in one Turbo (8 steps) edit, by span. Total kernel seconds at right. Lean port, DiT and VAE only, one profiled request per size on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. The unfilled end of each bar is all other kernels. The profiler slowed the 2048 request by 8 %.
kernel-classes: Small kernels take 226 of the QKV span's 542 ms. Milliseconds of GPU kernel time inside three spans of one Turbo edit at 1024, by kernel kind. Small kernels are elementwise ops, copies and layout conversions: norms, RoPE, activations, casts. Lean port, one profiled request, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
fit-32gb: Without the text encoder an edit peaks at 17 to 27 GiB, under a 32 GB card. Peak GPU memory in GiB during one Turbo (8 steps) edit, batch 1, bf16. Dashed line: the 32 GB RTX 5090, plotted as 32 GiB. Measured on the 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, not on a 5090. DiT and VAE only means text states were computed beforehand.
floor: On datasheet rates the same work takes 0.88 s; it takes 2.44 s. Milliseconds of GPU kernel time per span of one Turbo edit at 1024: measured, and the same work at two rates. Datasheet: 1 PFLOPS of bf16 tensor-core peak and 1,597 GB/s. Fastest measured: 422 TFLOP/s and 1,462 GB/s. Elementwise stages count as one read and one write. Lean port, one profiled request, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition.
ladder: 10 changes took a 1024² edit from 2.48 s to 1.01 s, 2.5 x faster. Milliseconds per Turbo (8 steps) edit at 1024², DiT + VAE, median of 5 warm requests, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. One change per row, in the order they were made. The last two steps miss the DINOv2 0.98 line on one and two of sixteen images; the last step is the earlier figure less its measured gain.
stages-then-now: The traced request drops 2.5 x at 1024² and 3.0 x at 2048². Milliseconds per Turbo (8 steps) edit request, by stage, DiT + VAE, one traced request per size. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. Stages do not add to the total; the rest is overhead. Glue reads 0 ms in the current build.
now-vs-baseline: Edits run 2.4 to 2.6 x faster than the port baseline; peak memory at 2048² is the one regression. Current build as a share of the port baseline, which is 100 %. Turbo (8 steps). Lower is better, except compute rate. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, edit, DiT + VAE unless the row says otherwise. The compute rate was measured on the 1,218 ms build, not the current default. The text encoder reads a 1024² copy of the input.
quality-gate: 14 of 16 1024² edits clear the 0.98 DINOv2 gate, and 16 of 16 at 2048². DINOv2 similarity of each edit to its frozen baseline image, per item. Axis zoomed to 0.97 to 1.00. Frozen set of 16 edits, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, Turbo (8 steps), edit, DiT + VAE. A VLM judge called item 0 identical and had no stable preference on item 4. Item 15 is the lettering poster.
vs-sglang: In-process, magpie takes 13 %, 19 % and 27 % less time than sglang's fastest working setup; its default takes 2.0 to 2.4 x as long over HTTP. Seconds per request, Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, median of 5 warm requests, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell on the same day. HTTP bars are curl totals and include PNG encoding and transfer. In-process bars are magpie's total and sglang's own encode, denoise and decode log, both with the text encoder. sglang's text stage was a conditioning-cache hit on a repeated prompt. Its default at 2048² in-process is 2.2 x magpie.
vs-sglang-memory: Magpie peaks below sglang's default in all three cases; sglang's fp8 build is lower at 1024², 19.5 against 25.9 GiB. Peak GPU memory in GiB, Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, same day. Magpie keeps a bf16 text encoder loaded; with its nvfp4 encoder it peaks at 16.5 GiB, 9.4 GiB lower. sglang's values are nvidia-smi memory used and magpie's are torch's peak allocated, so the two are not the same measure.
5090-latency: Magpie takes 46 % and 39 % less time than sglang's fastest setup; the official pipeline takes 20.7 x as long at 1024² and does not fit at 2048². Milliseconds per whole edit request, Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, median of 5 warm requests, one RTX 5090 (31.4 GiB). sglang[diffusion] 0.5.21, http time including png; magpie and diffusers are in-process. Magpie at 2048² parks the text encoder in host memory between requests, a 288 ms fetch inside its total. Bars past the axis end are cut and labelled.
5090-vs-pro6000: The RTX 5090 takes 19 to 23 % longer than the RTX PRO 6000 on magpie's requests. Milliseconds per whole request, Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, magpie in-process on each card, median of 5 warm requests. Different hosts: the PRO 6000 ran on Colab, the 5090 on RunPod. The 2048 pair is not like for like: the 5090 row stages the text encoder in host memory, a 288 ms fetch inside its total.
5090-memory: Magpie peaks at 26.35 GiB, under the 31.4 GiB card; at 2048² it keeps 8.6 GiB free with 4-bit attention and 5.0 GiB with 8-bit. Peak GPU memory in GiB, one Turbo (8 steps) request, batch 1, one RTX 5090. Dashed line: the card's usable 31.4 GiB. Magpie is torch's peak allocated; sglang is nvidia-smi memory used, as in the PRO 6000 comparison, so the two are not the same measure. sglang fp8 at 2048² is 0.05 GiB under the line.
5090-references: A 1024² edit takes 11 reference images with the encoder staged and 3 with it resident, under the 31.4 GiB card. Peak GPU memory (top) and DiT + VAE seconds (bottom) for one Turbo (8 steps) edit at 1024², against the number of reference images. RTX 5090. Dashed line: the card's 31.4 GiB usable. Each series ends at its most references. Staged ran out of memory at 12, resident at 4. At 2048² the staged encoder fits 1 reference and the resident encoder 0.
5090-cold-start: Evicting the model files from page cache adds 6.3 s to a cold start; the encoder load accounts for 3.6 s of it. Seconds from process start to each milestone on one RTX 5090. Each segment is the time between two milestones, left to right: imports, DiT + VAE, encoder, first image. Host dependent: this pod; an earlier 5090 host reached the first image in 8.4 s with the same files cached. The first-image segment matches the first request: 2,695 ms cached, 3,083 ms evicted.
tensor-core-ceiling: Torch bf16 runs at 93 % of its instruction ceiling; the 8-bit and 4-bit kernels reach 54 to 69 %, close to the 58 % and 55 % that operands streamed from global memory allow. TFLOP/s per number format on one RTX 5090: the instruction ceiling with operands in registers, read from shared memory, or streamed from global memory, against the kernel in use. Percent is of the register ceiling. Measured with native/peak.cu on 170 SMs. The bf16 kernel is torch's; the 8-bit and 4-bit kernels are CUTLASS, drawn at the high end of their range. The streamed bars sit below the kernels' high ends (708 and 1,209), so streaming at 128 × 128 does not on its own bound them. At 128 × 256 tiles the streamed rates are 624 and 1,243.
new-levers: Resuming the prefix cache saves 11 % of DiT + VAE time; a 1448 reference at 4-bit attention saves 16 % of a 2048 edit and passes the gate. DiT + VAE milliseconds per request on one RTX 5090, Turbo (8 steps). Top: a second, different edit of the same 1024 image. Bottom: a 2048 edit with a smaller reference image. Resumed against fresh: DINOv2 min 0.977, under the 0.98 line; median 0.9986; peak 17.59 GiB against 13.55 GiB. 2048 rows: the gate's 16 edits; DINOv2 min against the full-size output, 0.9757 to 0.9933. Against the frozen bf16 baseline, the 1024 reference fails the gate (DINOv2 >= 0.98, DreamSim <= 0.05); the others pass.
5090-staged-vs-resident: Staging the encoder adds 372 ms to a 1024² edit, 28 %, and is the only magpie mode that fits a 2048² edit on the card. Milliseconds per whole edit request by stage, Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, one RTX 5090. Resident idle 20.65 GiB against staged idle 5.47 GiB, the encoder in host memory. Fetch brings the encoder back from host memory; free releases it after the text pass. Segments too narrow for their value are unlabelled.
5090-memory-vs-latency-1024: Magpie is the fastest at 1024², 48 % less time than sglang's fastest build; its fastest edit peaks at 16.7 GiB, against 14.0 to 20.2 GiB for sglang. Each dot is one configuration: Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, one RTX 5090 with 31.4 GiB usable. Lower is better on both axes. Magpie's peak is torch's peak allocated, in process; sglang's is nvidia-smi memory used and its time is HTTP including PNG, so the two are not the same measure. At 1024², the lowest sglang peak is 14.0 GiB, from sglang fp8 + sage.
5090-memory-vs-latency-2048: Magpie is the fastest at 2048², 54 % less time than sglang's fastest build; its fastest edit peaks at 18.2 GiB, against 30.2 to 31.4 GiB for sglang. Each dot is one configuration: Turbo (8 steps), batch 1, one RTX 5090 with 31.4 GiB usable. Lower is better on both axes. Magpie's peak is torch's peak allocated, in process; sglang's is nvidia-smi memory used and its time is HTTP including PNG, so the two are not the same measure. At 2048², the lowest sglang peak is 30.2 GiB, from sglang default.
